---
title: "Git and GitHub"
description: "Learn Git with the Software Carpentry lesson, then make your first pull request to a lab repo."
---

Git tracks changes to your files; GitHub is where the lab keeps its repositories
and reviews each other's work. You'll learn Git from the Software Carpentry
lesson, then use this page for the part the lesson doesn't cover: how we work
together on GitHub. It ends with your first contribution to the lab, a pull
request to this wiki.

## Before you start

- Finish [The Unix Shell](https://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/) first;
  the Git lesson is taught from the command line.
- Have a GitHub account in the [Omnia-Lab-UC](https://github.com/Omnia-Lab-UC)
  organization (see [Welcome & First Steps](../onboarding/welcome.qmd)). You also
  need write access to the repo you're contributing to; if `git push` is
  rejected, ask Tomás.
- Install Git by following the lesson's
  [setup instructions](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/index.html#setup).

## 1. Work through the lesson

Do episodes 1–9 of
[Version Control with Git](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/). They take
you from your first commit to collaborating and resolving conflicts. A few notes
as you go:

- **Episode 7, [Remotes in GitHub](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/07-github.html):**
  set up the SSH key it walks you through. We clone lab repos over SSH.
- **Episode 8, [Collaborating](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/08-collab.html):**
  the lesson has both people push straight to `main`. That's fine for learning,
  but in the lab we work on branches and merge through pull requests instead
  (see below).
- **Episodes 10–13** (open science, licensing, citation, hosting) are short and
  worth reading, but you don't need them for your first contribution.
- **Episode 14, [Using Git from RStudio](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/14-supplemental-rstudio.html):**
  optional; useful if you work in R.

## 2. How we use GitHub in the lab

`main` is the shared version of a repo; for this wiki, it's the published site.
Rather than committing to it directly, we make changes on a branch and merge
them through a pull request, so someone else reviews them first:

1. Create a **branch** for your change.
2. Commit your work on the branch and push it to GitHub.
3. Open a **pull request** (PR) asking to merge your branch into `main`.
4. A labmate **reviews** it; you push more commits to address their comments.
5. Once it's approved, the **reviewer merges** it.

In commands:

```bash
git switch main
git pull                        # start from the latest main
git switch -c fix-welcome-typo  # create a branch and move to it
# ...edit files...
git add onboarding/welcome.qmd
git commit -m "Fix typo in welcome page"
git push -u origin fix-welcome-typo
```

After the push, Git prints a link to open a pull request. GitHub also shows a
**Compare & pull request** button on the repo page.

### Good pull requests

- **One change per PR.** Small PRs get reviewed faster; split unrelated changes
  into separate PRs.
- **Branch names** describe the change: `fix-welcome-typo`, `add-hpc-page`.
- **Title:** a short imperative summary, like a commit message:
  `Add HPC access page`.
- **Description:** what you changed and why, and anything the reviewer should
  look at closely.
- **Reviewer:** request your mentor from the *Reviewers* box on the PR page,
  unless you've agreed on someone else.
- **Feedback:** commit to the same branch and push; the PR updates itself. Reply
  to each comment so the reviewer knows it's been handled.
- **Checks:** some repos run automatic checks on every PR (this wiki rebuilds
  the whole site). If a check fails, click *Details* to see why, fix it on your
  branch, and push again.

### What never goes in a repo

Many lab repos are public, and anything you commit stays in the history even
after you delete the file. Never commit:

- passwords, API keys, tokens, or SSH keys;
- participant or patient data, or any data you don't have permission to share;
- unpublished results to a public repo;
- large data files. Keep data out of Git and list it in `.gitignore`
  (episode 6).

If you commit something sensitive by accident, tell your mentor right away.
Deleting it in a new commit isn't enough.

## 3. Your first pull request

Your first contribution is an improvement to this wiki.

1. **Pick a change.** Something you noticed while getting started: a typo, a
   broken or outdated link, a step that confused you, or a question you had to
   ask someone that the wiki should have answered. Pages marked *Stub* are fair
   game if you know the answer. Keep it small; if nothing comes to mind, ask
   your mentor.
2. **Clone the wiki** (only once):

   ```bash
   git clone git@github.com:Omnia-Lab-UC/lab_wiki.git
   cd lab_wiki
   ```

3. **Create a branch and make your edit**, following the
   [contributing guide](../contributing.qmd).
4. **Preview it** with `quarto preview` if you have
   [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) installed. Either way, the PR
   check rebuilds the site and fails if your change breaks it.
5. **Commit, push, and open a pull request**, and request your mentor as
   reviewer.
6. **Respond to the review** until it's approved and merged. Your change goes
   live on the wiki a few minutes after the merge.
7. **Clean up** your local copy:

   ```bash
   git switch main
   git pull
   git branch -d fix-welcome-typo
   ```

## Going further

- [Happy Git and GitHub for the useR](https://happygitwithr.com/): Git and
  GitHub from an R user's perspective, including RStudio setup and how to get
  unstuck.
- [About pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests):
  GitHub's documentation on pull requests and reviews.
